rv.q: Pacino and Cannavale are fierce and hilarious, rattling through the Mametspeak. But the entire cast blazes in Daniel Sullivan's tight, anger-unmanaged staging: David Harbour's humiliated office prick, Williamson; John C. McGinley's bilious Moss; Richard Schiff's schlemiel Aaronow; Jeremy Shamos's spineless Lingk; and Murphy Guyer's cop, Baylen.
The play, which runs less than two hours with an intermission, feels less furious than melancholy -- and, yes, more thoughtful -- this time around.
Cannavale is so good that, like his character, he can make us buy whatever he’s selling.
In short, I’m not sure I believe these men really work together.
That said, the drama often seems to be happening elsewhere, just beyond the proscenium, and not among the actors on stage, however individually adept.
Too bad its nasty punch is a tad soft here.
As the result, the play simmers when it wants to boil.
This performance places Shelly firmly and dominatingly at the center of “Glengarry,” which needs to be a tight ensemble piece.
This Glengarry Glen Ross is a reminder that when everything clicks in the theater—writing, acting, directing, design—the result can be transcendent.
Now in it’s second Broadway revival, "Glengarry" doesn’t quite hold up to the romance and ingenuity it once demonstrated.
It's not every day that you get to see such top-notch performers play hardball onstage, and their flashes of electricity sustain this imperfect Glengarry.
In Daniel Sullivan’s unevenly directed production, Pacino entertainingly holds the stage, winning laugh after laugh, but he makes a miscalculation fatal to the play’s core.
Pacino's instincts are too rich to let it pass him by, and, for a few minutes, you think that Sullivan's "Glengarry" will sear the play's soul.

Remember the good old days when David Mamet wrote muscular, expletive-filled dramas instead of lifeless, didactic polemics with stick figure characters? Last week, "The Anarchist," Mamet’s two-hander starring Patti LuPone as a prisoner and Debra Winger as her warden, opened to pans.

cn.t: Mamet's Pulitzer winner returns in a sluggish, uneven revival that disappoints despite its pedigree. Pacino's performance proves divisive, but Bobby Cannavale earns raves as the production's standout element.

vs.sum: The Gerald Schoenfeld Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions, although some side seats may have partial views. The sound quality is generally strong, enhancing the theatrical experience. However, the seating is tight, which can affect comfort, particularly for taller patrons. The theater's ambiance is charming with its historic character, and while facilities are adequate, expect some lines at the bar and restrooms.

acc.note: 7 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. Infrared devices available.
